Casino & gaming robots · buyer guide

Cover every shift on a floor that never closes.

The graveyard shift still needs drinks delivered, tables bussed, and floors cleaned — the hardest roles to keep. Beverage, F&B, cleaning, and delivery robots extend your coverage around the clock, deployed without disrupting play.

Casinos and gaming floors use four robot categories: beverage and floor-service robots that run drinks to players on the gaming floor; F&B service robots for the resort's restaurants and buffets; large-area scrubbers that clean gaming floors and public space around the clock; and delivery robots for the hotel tower. The buyer concern is a floor that never closes — deploying and servicing on a live 24/7 operation with zero disruption to play. Service Robot Co. picks the mix, finances it, deploys it without shutting the floor, and services it 24/7 nationwide.

What robots do in casinos & gaming

A casino-resort is a 24/7 hospitality operation at massive scale — a gaming floor, restaurants and bars, a hotel tower, and acres of public space, all running nonstop. Guest experience is the whole product, and it runs on service roles that are brutal to keep staffed across a 24-hour clock. Four robot categories carry that load: beverage and floor-service robots that keep players served on the gaming floor; F&B service robots that run food and bus tables across the resort's restaurants and buffets; large-area scrubbers that clean the gaming floor and public space without closing a section; and delivery robots for late-night amenity and room-service runs up in the hotel tower.

What makes a casino different is not the robot — it is the floor that never closes. The deployment has to be commissioned around a live 24/7 operation, run through dense crowds during peak play, and be serviced on the same clock the floor keeps, because a robot down at 3 a.m. cannot wait for a next-day visit. Get the fit, the routing around play, and the 24/7 service right, and one program standardizes beverage, F&B, cleaning, and delivery across every property. Get any of it wrong and it is an expensive cart parked off the floor.

What a casino floor actually needs from a robot

Before any model comparison, a casino-resort has constraints a warehouse or office deployment never faces. These are the ones that decide whether a program actually runs on a live floor.

  • Deploy without closing the floor — mapping, route-setting, and commissioning all happen around a live 24/7 operation. A deployment that needs a section shut down defeats the point.
  • Crowd-dense navigation — beverage, F&B, and cleaning robots all run through packed aisles during peak play. Routes are set around the busiest zones, not an empty room.
  • 24/7 service to match the floor — a robot down at 3 a.m. on a floor that never closes cannot wait for a next-day visit; uptime and a backup matter as much as the spec.
  • A property that spans gaming, dining, and a hotel — the right mix is beverage and cleaning on the gaming floor, F&B in the restaurants, and delivery in the tower, not a single SKU.
  • One program across properties — an operator group wants the same robot program running the same way at every property, with one partner accountable for all of it.

What Richtech's casino-resort beverage deployments actually proved

The high-profile casino beverage deployments — Richtech Robotics' ADAM units among the most visible — proved something useful: a robot on a gaming floor can be a guest-experience feature, not just back-of-house labor. Players noticed, and the floor kept serving through the shifts that are hardest to staff. What the photos do not show is the part that decides whether it works: the unit runs on a mapped route around live play, and it is only as reliable as the service behind it.

That is the honest read for an operator evaluating the category. The beverage robot is the delivery leg — it carries the drink a server still makes, across a large, crowded floor. The value is covering the walk on a graveyard shift you cannot staff, every night, without a call-out. Our casino beverage robots guide walks through which units are actually on floors today and what it takes to keep one running.

Buy vs. RaaS for a casino-resort or operator group

A gaming floor runs around the clock with no natural downtime window, and a property or operator group rarely wants a fleet of $16k–$96k machines landing as one capital hit. Robotics-as-a-Service folds the robot, the deploy-around-live-play commissioning, the 24/7 service, and a backup unit into one monthly cost — which is why most properties start there for beverage, F&B, and cleaning robots. Outright purchase fits a property with steady year-round utilization once a unit type is proven on the floor. We surface both, with the real total-cost math, in a site assessment.

The labor case for casino & gaming robots (illustrative)

The payback on a gaming floor is the graveyard and continuous-service shifts that are the hardest to keep staffed. A beverage or F&B robot on RaaS (~$335–$550/month) covers the drink and food runs across a large floor that would otherwise pull a server off their station on every trip, and it works the shifts turnover makes hardest to fill. A large-area scrubber on RaaS (~$600–$900/month for a mid-size unit) runs roughly 4–6× cheaper than a full-time overnight cleaner (~$3,500–$4,500/month all-in) on the open-floor portion of the job, and it runs the same route every night without a call-out.

The honest framing: this is coverage for the shifts you cannot reliably staff, not a headcount cut. The robot carries the repetitive floor and service work — the walking — so your beverage, F&B, and EVS teams cover the parts that need a person. Faster service keeps players at the machines and a spotless floor keeps the property premium. We build the real side-by-side in a site assessment.

When a casino robot is the wrong call

We would rather tell an operator no than sell a unit that sits parked off the floor. A casino or gaming robot is the wrong fit when:

  • The property is small enough that the floor and service are already covered in a normal shift — the scale that makes a robot pay off is not there yet.
  • The gaming floor is too tight or too densely packed for a unit to run a safe route even around peak play — we map it before we ever commit.
  • The property cannot commit to even a small pilot — one beverage route or one cleaning zone — to prove out before a program standardizes across the floor.
  • Nobody on site will own the daily basics (charging, docking, clearing a jam) — even a 24/7-serviced robot needs a local hand.
  • You want a robot that mixes and pours the drink — the beverage robot is the delivery leg; a bartender or server still makes it.

Why a casino should run a robot program through an integrator, not a bare OEM

A casino-resort is five hospitality businesses under one roof, running nonstop — gaming, beverage, dining, cleaning, and a hotel. An OEM sells one robot for one zone and ships a login. Everything that decides whether it runs on a live floor — picking the right unit, financing it without a single-property capital hit, commissioning around 24/7 play, connecting to POS and beverage systems, training beverage and EVS teams, and fixing it fast when it fails at 3 a.m. — is left to the property, usually across several vendors.

Service Robot Co. is the one partner for all of it, and OEM-neutral about which unit. We select the mix — beverage and cleaning on the floor, F&B in the restaurants, delivery in the tower — deploy it without shutting the floor, train your teams, and service it 24/7 through a US engineer network with a backup ready. Run an operator group? We standardize the same program across every property, with one partner accountable everywhere.

Common questions

What robots do casinos and gaming floors use?
Casinos use beverage and floor-service robots to run drinks to players on the gaming floor (e.g. Richtech ADAM, Pudu BellaBot, Bear Robotics Servi); F&B service robots for the resort's restaurants and buffets; large-area scrubbers to clean gaming floors and public space around the clock (e.g. Gausium Scrubber 75, Avidbots Neo, Pudu CC1); and delivery robots for hotel-tower amenity and room service. The right mix depends on your property and floor layout.
Can you deploy without shutting down the gaming floor?
Yes. We commission around a live 24/7 operation — mapping, route-setting, and rollout happen without closing sections or interrupting play.
Will a beverage robot keep up on a packed gaming floor?
We only select units that navigate dense crowds and tight aisles, and we set service routes around your busiest zones before anything goes live — so it moves with the floor, not against it. The robot covers the walk; a server still makes the drink.
The floor runs 24/7 — what happens when a robot goes down at 3 a.m.?
Our service matches your hours: 24/7 uptime and dispatch backed by a US service-engineer network, with a backup unit ready. A down robot is our problem, around the clock — not your floor manager's.
Can the robots integrate with our POS and beverage systems?
Where it pays off, yes. We connect robots to POS, beverage, and hotel systems during deployment so they fit how your floor already runs instead of sitting outside it.
